story: Build one filmable cause-and-effect story around the exact requested subject. Lock a visible goal, a physical constraint, a change of technique, and a payoff that resolves the opening. Keep one primary subject, one location, and a consistent prop and lighting bible. Each shot must change the food or situation. Do not invent records, prices, superlatives, or unavailable ingredients. If a claim needs evidence, mark it for review instead of saying it as fact.
foodStory: Treat the recipe as a physical transformation: preparation, heat or mixing, assembly, and serving. Prefer appetizing, plausible details: browning, bubbling fat, steam, crisp edge, glossy glaze, soft crumb, short cheese stretch, sauce cling, or clean knife cut when the ingredients support them. Show a real technique and the changed result; avoid magic cooking, raw-to-finished jumps inside a take, excessive smoke, infinite cheese, impossible utensils, and unrelated beauty shots. For a recipe guide, show each measured ingredient as it enters the same pan, keep a usable ingredient list and full method, then cut across the real cooking time before serving. The first finished-food tease is a deliberate preview; the later preparation starts clean. Never imply that generated footage is proof a recipe was cooked or tasted.
shot: Write one distinct continuous moving event. The still shows its start state; the motion starts there, changes a visible ingredient or object, and ends at a state that can connect to the next shot. Specify the subject, hand or tool, direction, material response, and one restrained camera move following the action. Repeat the visual bible's set and key props without overloading the model. Keep hands anatomically plausible and tools in contact with food. Never ask for multiple cuts or a static zoom. Align the requested motion to the actual start frame: if a spoon is already holding a dumpling above the pan, ask it to rise slightly or hold, never lower it back into food while pretending it is a new lift. Keep the food item intact in every frame; test a short pilot before extending a difficult hand-and-food action.
sound: Name only sounds caused by visible actions, such as crisp tear, quiet sizzle, spoon scrape, pour, bite, or plate tap. Leave space for natural kitchen room tone. A music bed is optional and must be licensed for the intended platform. Do not copy the reference video's soundtrack. When the scenario requests recordings-only, every cue needs a provenance-tagged recording of the matching physical action. Omit any unsupported cue and block release until the actual mix is heard.
footage: Prefer native moving footage of physical food change. Build each shot around one action the model can execute: a single hand, one tool, one food target, a start state and an end state. Lock the set, plate, ingredients and light before generation. Use a finish-state reference only after verifying it matches the previous shot. Reject food morphs, floating tools, duplicated hands and motion that is only a camera push over a still.
montage: Cut on the physical action or sound transient. Alternate a wide establishing view with close texture views only when geography remains clear. The opening may tease the finished food; the later shots must earn that payoff through preparation and heat. Let an ingredient, hand direction, plate position or audio cue bridge adjacent shots. Use transitions sparingly when they express a time or place change; a hard cut is often clearer for continuous cooking. Preserve the same story time and final duration when applying dissolves, grade, title and seal. Balance music under close kitchen sound and narration; do not infer a good mix from loudness numbers alone.
review: Before spending GPU time, reject title-topic mismatch, unsupported price or record claim, repeated format-set-hook combination, missing physical action, inconsistent set or prop, shot-duration mismatch, and an ending that does not resolve the opening. After rendering, inspect actual frames and listen to actual audio; technical metrics alone cannot establish quality.
